source.title: Beyond SAEs: Consistent Concept Discovery with Sparse Coding
source.authors: Jin-Ho Choi; Hyesu Lim; Jaegul Choo; Steffen Schneider

record.tranche_reason: The study measures cross-seed agreement of SAE dictionaries and codes, and evaluates information localized in a small number of SAE latents. These are conceptual tests of dictionary-feature stability and sparse concept localization, not a reproduction of toy-model superposition.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results for its own synthetic recovery experiments, foundation-model SAE consistency measurements, and sparse probing. It does not train toy networks to test whether they form superposed representations. Cited results from other studies are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: This is mainly a methods paper for ConSDL. It still measures cross-seed decoder and coefficient agreement for six standard SAE architectures and ConSDL on four real backbones, plus how atoms split as dictionary size grows. Both bear directly on whether dictionary features are stable, canonical units (V5). It does not train toy networks, test capacity accounts, compare features with neurons, or test feature dimensionality.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that standard SAEs learn seed-dependent dictionaries and that ConSDL improves cross-seed dictionary and coefficient consistency (+17.6% DCS, +35.9% MCC over the baseline average) and achieves near-perfect synthetic recovery. They also report that larger ConSDL dictionaries capture finer-grained concepts. They caveat that there is no real-model ground truth, that the models are small, and that a sparse linear representation is assumed.
record.recipe_differences: The study develops and evaluates ConSDL, using per-sample FISTA sparse coding, coefficient refitting, and co-active similarity regularization. It does not reproduce the Toy Models of Superposition setup or its intervention and measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: Results are reported across dictionary expansions and sparsity levels; the paper also reports that consistency gains vary with these settings and that higher sparsity levels yield smaller gains in the consistent-atom analysis.

fits_no_version.finding: On synthetic sparse mixtures, standard SAEs' ground-truth dictionary and coefficient recovery falls sharply as dictionary size and Zipf frequency imbalance grow. ConSDL recovers near-perfectly across all 16 settings. Cross-seed DCS correlates with recovery (r=0.90).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE recovery of known sparse dictionaries depends on dictionary size and feature-frequency imbalance, and cross-seed consistency tracks recovery.

fits_no_version.finding: One- and five-latent sparse probes reach AUROC 0.73–0.79 on SAE-Probes, similar across SAE methods.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Task information is localized in a few dictionary latents regardless of SAE architecture.

record.problems: Real foundation-model decompositions have no ground truth in this study, so cross-seed agreement is only a consistency measure. The authors note that their experiments use relatively small models and do not establish whether the gains extend to models with billions of parameters. The reported Table 8 variability is across width/sparsity settings rather than training seeds.
record.rows_left_out: No rows were omitted. Table 8 backbone summaries were used rather than extracting every configuration from Tables 15–18; sparse-probing rows use the reported 16× results in Table 10.

untested.parts: All of it. The synthetic data are generated sparse mixtures used to test SAE recovery; no toy network is trained.
All of it. Capacity competition and dedicated versus shared dimensions are not studied.
There is no comparison of features with neurons and no evidence of more features than dimensions in the backbones. Sparse probing is method evaluation only.
Completeness of SAE features and whether they are the model's own units, as opposed to reproducible decompositions. The authors note there is no ground truth for real models.
All of it. The authors explicitly set aside nonlinear or manifold features.

missing.what: Cross-seed DCS, MCC and usable-atom fraction for the six baseline SAEs, per backbone and averaged. For example, the all-backbone DCS averages are Matryoshka 0.53, ReLU 0.74 and MP-SAE 0.82 (MCC 0.49).
Atom-level cross-seed consistency distributions, showing many low-consistency baseline atoms, especially in vision. Selected TopK atoms match at about 0.19–0.24.
Cross-method one-to-many correspondence: baseline atoms often map to several ConSDL atoms, so different methods yield different units.
Duplicate atoms inflate DCS. Deduplication lowers DCS from 0.85 to 0.78 on CLIP without similarity regularization.

record.verdict_notes: Rows r1–r8 are the study's own method compared with others. The evidence most relevant to V5, the baseline SAE inconsistency, is not in the rows and should be added. Sparse-probing rows were unlinked from V4 because they evaluate the method rather than test superposition in the model.

versions.untested_parts: Whether trained toy networks store excess sparse features as overlapping, nearly orthogonal directions; the proposed sparsity-dependent transition and regular geometry. Synthetic data have known sparse decompositions, but the experiments measure SAE recovery of those decompositions rather than spontaneous superposition in a toy network.
Whether polysemanticity is caused by capacity competition, or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions while others share.
Whether polysemanticity arises through mechanisms other than capacity pressure.

The study does not compare features with individual neurons, establish ground-truth feature recovery in real models, or test models larger than the relatively small backbones studied. Sparse probing tests class/task information in a few SAE latents, not recovery of a known real-model decomposition.
The study measures cross-seed consistency and some changes in feature granularity, but not whether SAE features are complete or uniquely canonical units of the underlying model.

Whether the underlying superposed features are intrinsically one-dimensional directions or multidimensional objects. Atom correspondences and semantic examples do not establish intrinsic feature dimensionality.

rows.operation_detail: Measured cross-seed decoder cosine similarity (DCS) and mean coefficient correlation (MCC); Table 8 averages over nine dictionary-width and sparsity settings.
rows.baseline: Six SAE baselines; per-backbone baseline-average value not stated
rows.uncertainty: ±0.07 across nine expansion/sparsity settings, not across seeds
rows.note: The paper reports three seeds and averages consistency over seed pairs. This is evidence of cross-seed decoder-direction agreement, not proof of canonical or complete features.
rows.check: This is the study's own method compared with others, so treat it as a best-case value. DCS 0.78 means cross-seed agreement is substantial but incomplete. The authors say real-model consistency stays below the near-perfect synthetic recovery, so 'observed' overstates it.

rows.operation_detail: Compared consistent atoms across dictionary sizes using cross-seed cosine similarity and decoder-direction matching.

conditions.value: CLIP ViT-B/16, DINOv2-B/14, Pythia-160M, GPT-2 Small

rows.measure: Fraction of consistent 4× ConSDL atoms with at least two consistent 16× counterparts
rows.note: The authors interpret the one-to-many correspondences as larger dictionaries representing some broader concepts with multiple, more specific atoms. This bears on stability/canonicality but does not determine intrinsic feature dimensionality.
rows.check: Measured on consistent atoms only (cross-seed ≥0.7), with counterparts defined at decoder cosine ≥0.7. About half of 4× atoms split into several 16× atoms (ReLU 12–37%), so atom identity depends on dictionary size. This qualifies canonicality rather than confirming it.

source_check.correct: The comparison is 4× dictionaries at ℓ0 ≈ 32 versus 16× dictionaries at ℓ0 ≈ 128. The reported 45–55% for ConSDL and 12–37% for ReLU use consistent atoms and counterpart cosine thresholds ≥0.7.
source_check.locator_found: Section E.2, One-to-many correspondence across dictionary sizes; Figure 15 caption
source_check.problem: The conditions omit the simultaneous sparsity change, preventing attribution of the correspondence differences to dictionary width alone.

relationships.condition: Standard SAE architectures (ReLU, TopK, BatchTopK, Matryoshka, MP-SAE, iSAE) on CLIP, DINOv2, Pythia-160M and GPT-2 Small
relationships.reason: Based on the text, as no row records this. In Table 8, baseline averages across backbones are DCS 0.53–0.82 and MCC 0.43–0.69. CLIP 16× ReLU DCS is as low as 0.33, and many baseline atoms have low cross-seed consistency (Fig. 4A). Stability depends on architecture, width and sparsity.
relationships.display_finding: Baseline averages across backbones were DCS 0.53–0.82 and MCC 0.43–0.69, with CLIP 16× ReLU as low as 0.33 DCS, and many atoms had low cross-seed consistency that varied with architecture, width and sparsity.

relation.reason: Its cross-seed consistency and cross-size correspondence experiments directly test stability and canonical identity in V5.

tranche.reason: The study directly qualifies V5 through measured seed dependence, incomplete consistency and extraction-setting dependence of dictionary atoms. These are results that the stable, canonical-unit claim needs restating.

source_check.notes: Table 8 uncertainties describe variation across nine width/sparsity settings, not training seeds. ConSDL values assess the authors' own method; real-model ground-truth completeness is unavailable.

statements.correction: Across four backbones, 45–55% of consistent ConSDL atoms at 4× and ℓ0 ≈ 32 have at least two consistent counterparts at 16× and ℓ0 ≈ 128; consistency and counterpart thresholds are ≥0.7. Section E.2; Figure 15.
statements.problem: The 45–55% result is correct, but the comparison changes sparsity as well as width and therefore does not isolate width sensitivity.
